claim: VIP interneurons in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) are highly correlated with locomotion.
source: Although VIP neuron activity in the primary visual cortex (V1) of mouse is highly correlated with locomotion, the relevance of locomotion-related VIP neuron activity to visual coding is not known.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: VIP neurons in mouse V1 respond strongly to low contrast front-to-back motion that is congruent with self-motion during locomotion.
source: Here we show that VIP neurons in mouse V1 respond strongly to low contrast front-to-back motion that is congruent with self-motion during locomotion but are suppressed by other directions and contrasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: VIP neurons are suppressed by other directions and contrasts.
source: Here we show that VIP neurons in mouse V1 respond strongly to low contrast front-to-back motion that is congruent with self-motion during locomotion but are suppressed by other directions and contrasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: VIP and SST neurons have complementary contrast tuning.
source: VIP and SST neurons have complementary contrast tuning.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Layer 2/3 contains a substantially larger population of low contrast preferring pyramidal neurons than deeper layers.
source: Layer 2/3 contains a substantially larger population of low contrast preferring pyramidal neurons than deeper layers, and layer 2/3 (but not deeper layer) pyramidal neurons show bias for front-to-back motion specifically at low contrast.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2e.

claim: Layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons show bias for front-to-back motion specifically at low contrast.
source: Layer 2/3 contains a substantially larger population of low contrast preferring pyramidal neurons than deeper layers, and layer 2/3 (but not deeper layer) pyramidal neurons show bias for front-to-back motion specifically at low contrast.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2c.

claim: Deeper layer pyramidal neurons do not show bias for front-to-back motion at low contrast.
source: Layer 2/3 contains a substantially larger population of low contrast preferring pyramidal neurons than deeper layers, and layer 2/3 (but not deeper layer) pyramidal neurons show bias for front-to-back motion specifically at low contrast.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2c.

claim: VIP-SST mutual antagonism regulates the gain of the cortex to achieve sensitivity to specific weak stimuli without compromising network stability.
source: Network modeling indicates that VIP-SST mutual antagonism regulates the gain of the cortex to achieve sensitivity to specific weak stimuli without compromising network stability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by modeling results in Figure 5.

claim: VIP interneurons regulate feedback inhibition of pyramidal neurons through suppression of SST interneurons.
source: In the superficial layers of the cortex, vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing (VIP) interneurons regulate feedback inhibition of pyramidal neurons through suppression of Martinotti-type somatostatin-expressing (SST) interneurons (Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: SST neurons inhibit VIP neurons.
source: Vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing (VIP) interneurons in the cortex regulate feedback inhibition of pyramidal neurons through suppression of somatostatin-expressing (SST) interneurons and, reciprocally, SST neurons inhibit VIP neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: VIP neurons in mouse V1 are reliably active during periods of locomotion.
source: Through this disinhibitory mechanism, VIP interneurons are believed to modulate network dynamics based on the behavioral state of the animal; for instance, VIP neurons in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) are reliably active during periods of locomotion (Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2014.

claim: VIP neurons in V1 are a target of top-down inputs and mediate enhancement of local pyramidal cell activity in response to activation of those inputs.
source: Moreover, VIP neurons in V1 are a target of top-down inputs and mediate enhancement of local pyramidal cell activity in response to activation of those inputs (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Mouse V1 is necessary for the detection of low contrast visual stimuli.
source: Behaviorally, mouse V1 is necessary for the detection of low contrast visual stimuli (Glickfeld et al., 2013), and the optogenetic activation of VIP neurons in mouse V1 lowers contrast detection thresholds whereas the activation of SST or PV neurons raises it (Cone et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Glickfeld et al., 2013.

claim: Optogenetic activation of VIP neurons in mouse V1 lowers contrast detection thresholds.
source: Behaviorally, mouse V1 is necessary for the detection of low contrast visual stimuli (Glickfeld et al., 2013), and the optogenetic activation of VIP neurons in mouse V1 lowers contrast detection thresholds whereas the activation of SST or PV neurons raises it (Cone et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cone et al., 2019.

claim: Activation of SST or PV neurons raises contrast detection thresholds.
source: Behaviorally, mouse V1 is necessary for the detection of low contrast visual stimuli (Glickfeld et al., 2013), and the optogenetic activation of VIP neurons in mouse V1 lowers contrast detection thresholds whereas the activation of SST or PV neurons raises it (Cone et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cone et al., 2019.

claim: The perception of low contrast stimuli is strongly enhanced by VIP neuron activity in V1.
source: This suggests that the perception of low contrast stimuli is strongly enhanced by VIP neuron activity in V1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on contrast detection thresholds.

claim: VIP neuron activity has been shown to be suppressed below baseline in response to high contrast full-field grating stimuli of all tested spatial and temporal frequencies.
source: Although the activity of VIP neurons has been shown to be suppressed below baseline in response to high contrast full-field grating stimuli of all tested spatial and temporal frequencies (de Vries et al., 2020), the responses of VIP neurons to low contrast visual stimuli are not known.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Vries et al., 2020.

claim: SST neurons responded exclusively at high contrast.
source: SST neurons responded exclusively at high contrast whereas VIP neurons responded exclusively at low contrast with a strong preference for front-to-back motion that is congruent with self-motion during locomotion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: VIP neurons responded exclusively at low contrast with a strong preference for front-to-back motion that is congruent with self-motion during locomotion.
source: SST neurons responded exclusively at high contrast whereas VIP neurons responded exclusively at low contrast with a strong preference for front-to-back motion that is congruent with self-motion during locomotion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figures 1-3.

claim: As a population, layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons responded more strongly at low contrast than high contrast.
source: As a population, layer 2/3 – but not deeper layer – pyramidal neurons responded more strongly at low contrast than high contrast and showed a slight, but significant, bias for front-to-back motion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons showed a slight, but significant, bias for front-to-back motion.
source: As a population, layer 2/3 – but not deeper layer – pyramidal neurons responded more strongly at low contrast than high contrast and showed a slight, but significant, bias for front-to-back motion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 2c.

claim: Deeper layer pyramidal neurons did not respond more strongly at low contrast than high contrast.
source: As a population, layer 2/3 – but not deeper layer – pyramidal neurons responded more strongly at low contrast than high contrast and showed a slight, but significant, bias for front-to-back motion.
evidence: This is implied by the contrast with layer 2/3 and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: VIP-driven disinhibition at low contrast can drive large increases in pyramidal neuron activity, despite the relatively low activity of both SST and pyramidal neurons in this contrast regime.
source: Finally, we made novel extensions of stabilized supralinear network (SSN) models to incorporate the diversity of inhibitory interneuron types and used these models to demonstrate that VIP-driven disinhibition at low contrast can drive large increases in pyramidal neuron activity, despite the relatively low activity of both SST and pyramidal neurons in this contrast regime.
evidence: This is a primary finding from modeling stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The selective enhancement of front-to-back motion could increase the detection of obstacles approaching head-on during locomotion.
source: The selective enhancement of front-to-back motion could increase the detection of obstacles approaching head-on during locomotion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: VIP neurons amplify responses of pyramidal neurons to weak but behaviorally-relevant stimuli.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that VIP neurons amplify responses of pyramidal neurons to weak but behaviorally-relevant stimuli.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the introduction, based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The majority of neurons were responsive to the stimulus set.
source: The majority of neurons were responsive to the stimulus set (Figure 2a), measured as a statistically significant bias in responses depending on grating contrast and direction (bootstrapped χ2test, p<0.01; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Virtually all VIP neurons responded only at low (<20%) contrast to front-to-back motion (0 degrees; nasal-to-temporal) or an adjacent direction.
source: Virtually all VIP neurons responded only at low (<20%) contrast to front-to-back motion (0 degrees; nasal-to-temporal) or an adjacent direction (Figure 2b), yielding the greatest direction bias among Cre lines as quantified by the vector sum of direction preferences (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figures 2b and 2c.

claim: VIP neurons yielded the greatest direction bias among Cre lines as quantified by the vector sum of direction preferences.
source: Virtually all VIP neurons responded only at low (<20%) contrast to front-to-back motion (0 degrees; nasal-to-temporal) or an adjacent direction (Figure 2b), yielding the greatest direction bias among Cre lines as quantified by the vector sum of direction preferences (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The direction of bias was consistent across all Vip mice.
source: The direction of bias was consistent across all Vip mice (n = 6 sessions, 3 mice; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and did not result from stimulus direction-selective running behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The direction bias did not result from stimulus direction-selective running behavior.
source: The direction of bias was consistent across all Vip mice (n = 6 sessions, 3 mice; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and did not result from stimulus direction-selective running behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: High contrast gratings of all directions significantly suppressed activity in a substantial fraction of VIP neurons.
source: High contrast gratings of all directions significantly suppressed activity in a substantial fraction of VIP neurons whereas such suppression was rare in other Cre lines (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Suppression by high contrast gratings was rare in other Cre lines.
source: High contrast gratings of all directions significantly suppressed activity in a substantial fraction of VIP neurons whereas such suppression was rare in other Cre lines (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: SST neurons had high contrast selectivity, weak direction and orientation selectivity, and varied direction preference.
source: SST neurons had high contrast selectivity, weak direction and orientation selectivity, and varied direction preference (Figure 2b,e,g,h), resulting in an average population response that was strong at high contrast across all directions, complementing the non-direction selective suppression at high contrast observed in VIP neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2b, e, g, h.

claim: SST neurons had an average population response that was strong at high contrast across all directions.
source: SST neurons had high contrast selectivity, weak direction and orientation selectivity, and varied direction preference (Figure 2b,e,g,h), resulting in an average population response that was strong at high contrast across all directions, complementing the non-direction selective suppression at high contrast observed in VIP neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Pyramidal neurons exhibited substantial direction and orientation selectivity and tiled all eight possible direction preferences.
source: Unlike inhibitory interneurons, pyramidal neurons exhibited substantial direction and orientation selectivity and tiled all eight possible direction preferences (Figure 2b,g,h).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2b, g, h.

claim: Nearly all VIP neurons were low contrast-preferring.
source: This analysis confirmed that nearly all VIP neurons were low contrast-preferring and nearly all SST neurons were high contrast-preferring (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Nearly all SST neurons were high contrast-preferring.
source: This analysis confirmed that nearly all VIP neurons were low contrast-preferring and nearly all SST neurons were high contrast-preferring (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Contrast preference among pyramidal neurons systematically varied across cortical layers, exhibiting a progression from a mixture of low and high contrast-preferring neurons in layer 2/3 to almost exclusively high contrast-preferring neurons in layers 5 and 6.
source: Contrast preference among pyramidal neurons systematically varied across cortical layers, exhibiting a progression from a mixture of low and high contrast-preferring neurons in layer 2/3 to almost exclusively high contrast-preferring neurons in layers 5 and 6.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in layer 2/3 showed direction bias toward front-to-back motion at 5% and 10% contrast but not at higher contrasts.
source: Like VIP neurons, pyramidal neurons in layer 2/3 showed direction bias toward front-to-back motion at 5% and 10% contrast but not at higher contrasts (Figure 2c); pyramidal neurons in deeper layers did not have direction bias.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in deeper layers did not have direction bias.
source: Like VIP neurons, pyramidal neurons in layer 2/3 showed direction bias toward front-to-back motion at 5% and 10% contrast but not at higher contrasts (Figure 2c); pyramidal neurons in deeper layers did not have direction bias.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Concerted changes in response magnitude near 20% contrast across all Cre lines and layers indicate the presence of a phase transition in cortical dynamics between a low contrast regime exemplified by relatively inactive SST neurons and a high contrast regime exemplified by highly active SST neurons.
source: Taken together, concerted changes in response magnitude near 20% contrast across all Cre lines and layers indicate the presence of a phase transition in cortical dynamics between a low contrast regime exemplified by relatively inactive SST neurons and a high contrast regime exemplified by highly active SST neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data stated in the results.

claim: The Vip and Sst Cre lines label all transcriptomic subtypes of VIP and SST neurons, respectively.
source: The Vip and Sst Cre lines label all transcriptomic subtypes of VIP and SST neurons, respectively, suggesting that common subtypes of SST neurons, such as Martinotti-type SST neurons, are all high contrast-preferring and common subtypes of VIP neurons are all low contrast-preferring.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a reference to Tasic et al., 2018.

claim: Common subtypes of SST neurons, such as Martinotti-type SST neurons, are all high contrast-preferring.
source: The Vip and Sst Cre lines label all transcriptomic subtypes of VIP and SST neurons, respectively, suggesting that common subtypes of SST neurons, such as Martinotti-type SST neurons, are all high contrast-preferring and common subtypes of VIP neurons are all low contrast-preferring.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the Cre line labeling data.

claim: Common subtypes of VIP neurons are all low contrast-preferring.
source: The Vip and Sst Cre lines label all transcriptomic subtypes of VIP and SST neurons, respectively, suggesting that common subtypes of SST neurons, such as Martinotti-type SST neurons, are all high contrast-preferring and common subtypes of VIP neurons are all low contrast-preferring.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the Cre line labeling data.

claim: The Cux2 and Rorb Cre lines label all transcriptomic excitatory neuron types in layers 2/3 and 4, respectively.
source: Furthermore, the Cux2 and Rorb Cre lines label all transcriptomic excitatory neuron types in layers 2/3 and 4, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a reference to Tasic et al., 2018.

claim: Neurons of the same transcriptomic subtype can differ in contrast preference.
source: Our finding of substantial populations of both high contrast-preferring and low contrast-preferring neurons in layer 4, where there is only a single transcriptomic excitatory neuron type, demonstrates that neurons of the same transcriptomic subtype can differ in contrast preference.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the contrast preference data and transcriptomic data.

claim: VIP neurons are a major source of suppressed-by-contrast (SbC) neurons in V1.
source: Consistent with a recent report (de Vries et al., 2020), these results identify VIP neurons as a major source of SbC neurons in V1.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2d and a citation to de Vries et al., 2020.

claim: SbC neurons are not suppressed at low contrast but exhibit robust visual responses to front-to-back motion in such conditions.
source: Surprisingly, we observe that not only are these SbC neurons not suppressed at low contrast but that they exhibit robust visual responses to front-to-back motion in such conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figures 1-3.

claim: VIP neurons are suppressed below baseline in response to high contrast gratings, rather than suppressed to baseline.
source: The finding that VIP neurons are suppressed below baseline in response to high contrast gratings, rather than suppressed to baseline, might be due to the high spontaneous activity of VIP neurons that is available to be suppressed compared to the other neuron types measured here (see Figure 3 as well as Extended Data Figure 1 of de Vries et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3 and a citation to de Vries et al., 2020.

claim: The high spontaneous activity of VIP neurons enables the cortical circuit to raise or lower the amount of disinhibition of pyramidal neurons depending on stimulus contrast.
source: Our measurements of contrast tuning suggest that the high spontaneous activity of VIP neurons enables the cortical circuit to raise or lower the amount of disinhibition of pyramidal neurons depending on stimulus contrast.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the contrast tuning data.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in layers 2/3 and 4, as well as VIP and SST interneurons, had increased activity during stimulus presentations when the mouse was running compared with stimulus presentations when the mouse was stationary.
source: Pyramidal neurons in layers 2/3 and 4, as well as VIP and SST interneurons, had increased activity during stimulus presentations when the mouse was running compared with stimulus presentations when the mouse was stationary (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The low contrast and front-to-back direction selectivity that was common to nearly all VIP neurons resulted in an average VIP population response that had tuning closely resembling the tuning of any individual VIP neuron.
source: During locomotion, the low contrast and front-to-back direction selectivity that was common to nearly all VIP neurons resulted in an average VIP population response that had tuning closely resembling the tuning of any individual VIP neuron (Figure 3, first column).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The VIP population only weakly responded to front-to-back motion at low contrast when the mice were stationary and did not respond to gratings of any other direction or contrast.
source: By comparison, the VIP population only weakly responded to front-to-back motion at low contrast when the mice were stationary and did not respond to gratings of any other direction or contrast.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Running increased the SST population response to high contrast gratings.
source: Running also increased the SST population response to high contrast gratings, which also had the highest average response to front-to-back motion but responded strongly as a population to other directions as well (Figure 3, second column).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The SST population had the highest average response to front-to-back motion but responded strongly as a population to other directions as well.
source: Running also increased the SST population response to high contrast gratings, which also had the highest average response to front-to-back motion but responded strongly as a population to other directions as well (Figure 3, second column).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The pyramidal population in layer 2/3 (CUX2) responded broadly across directions but more strongly at low than high contrast.
source: The pyramidal population in layer 2/3 (CUX2) responded broadly across directions but more strongly at low than high contrast (Figure 3, third column), whereas the pyramidal population in layer 4 (RORB) had comparable response magnitude and running enhancement across contrasts (Figure 3, fourth column).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The pyramidal population in layer 4 (RORB) had comparable response magnitude and running enhancement across contrasts.
source: The pyramidal population in layer 2/3 (CUX2) responded broadly across directions but more strongly at low than high contrast (Figure 3, third column), whereas the pyramidal population in layer 4 (RORB) had comparable response magnitude and running enhancement across contrasts (Figure 3, fourth column).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is a substantial enhancement of responses to low contrast visual stimuli during locomotion that is specific to layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons and VIP neurons.
source: This analysis demonstrates a substantial enhancement of responses to low contrast visual stimuli during locomotion that is specific to layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons and VIP neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: VIP neurons have the highest weights for blank sweep, low contrasts (5–20%), running, directions of 0° and 180°, running by direction interactions at 0° and 45°, and direction by contrast interactions at ±45° and low contrasts.
source: VIP neurons had the highest weights for blank sweep, low contrasts (5–20%), running, directions of 0° and 180°, running by direction interactions at 0° and 45°, and direction by contrast interactions at ±45° and low contrasts (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: SST neurons have the highest weights for high contrasts (40–80%), direction of 0°, and running by direction interactions at all directions.
source: SST neurons had the highest weights for high contrasts (40–80%), direction of 0°, and running by direction interactions at all directions (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons have significant weights only for running, low contrasts (5–20%), and all directions.
source: Layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons have significant weights only for running, low contrasts (5–20%), and all directions (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The GLM analysis confirms the influence of running, stimulus direction, and stimulus contrast but suggests that interactions among these variables is limited.
source: Overall, this analysis confirms the influence of running, stimulus direction, and stimulus contrast but suggests that interactions among these variables is limited.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: VIP neurons disinhibit pyramidal neurons through their inhibition of SST neurons.
source: Anatomical and optogenetic perturbation experiments suggest that VIP neurons disinhibit pyramidal neurons through their inhibition of SST neurons (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014; Pi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to Pfeffer et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014; Pi et al., 2013.

claim: Visual cortex has higher gain at low contrast than high contrast.
source: Evidence that visual cortex has higher gain at low contrast than high contrast (Heuer and Britten, 2002; Cavanaugh et al., 2002; Carandini and Heeger, 2012) suggests that a small reduction in feedback inhibition (e.g. disinhibition) is capable of driving a large increase in pyramidal neuron activity (Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to Heuer and Britten, 2002; Cavanaugh et al., 2002; Carandini and Heeger, 2012.

claim: A small reduction in feedback inhibition (e.g. disinhibition) is capable of driving a large increase in pyramidal neuron activity.
source: Evidence that visual cortex has higher gain at low contrast than high contrast (Heuer and Britten, 2002; Cavanaugh et al., 2002; Carandini and Heeger, 2012) suggests that a small reduction in feedback inhibition (e.g. disinhibition) is capable of driving a large increase in pyramidal neuron activity (Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2019.

claim: VIP neurons are essential to establishing the high gain regime at low contrast as a result of VIP-mediated disinhibition forming a positive feedback loop that depends upon, and contributes to, network dynamics.
source: We hypothesized that VIP neurons are essential to establishing the high gain regime at low contrast as a result of VIP-mediated disinhibition forming a positive feedback loop (i.e. Pyr → VIP → SST → Pyr) that depends upon, and contributes to, network dynamics.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results.

claim: Stabilized supralinear network (SSN) models have been proposed to account for a variety of contrast-dependent response properties in visual cortex.
source: Stabilized supralinear network (SSN) models have been proposed to account for a variety of contrast-dependent response properties in visual cortex (Rubin et al., 2015; Ahmadian et al., 2013), including the transition from a high gain regime at low contrast to a feedback inhibition dominated low gain regime at high contrast (Adesnik, 2017; Sanzeni et al., 2020), as well as cortical noise correlations (Hennequin et al., 2018), surround suppression (Liu et al., 2018), and effects of feature and spatial attention on neural activity (Lindsay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The model is able to qualitatively reproduce the population direction and contrast tuning observed for VIP, SST, and layer 2/3 pyramidal (CUX2) neurons.
source: This model is able to qualitatively reproduce the population direction and contrast tuning we observed for VIP, SST, and layer 2/3 pyramidal (CUX2) neurons as well as make a prediction for the tuning of PV neurons (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Model VIP neurons are suppressed at high levels of external input regardless of stimulus direction, reproducing the suppressed-by-contrast behavior observed in imaging experiments.
source: Model VIP neurons are suppressed at high levels of external input regardless of stimulus direction, reproducing the suppressed-by-contrast behavior we observed in our imaging experiments, and active for all stimulus direction at low contrast but most active for the zero degrees direction, again reproducing VIP neuron tuning (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Model VIP neurons are active for all stimulus direction at low contrast but most active for the zero degrees direction.
source: Model VIP neurons are suppressed at high levels of external input regardless of stimulus direction, reproducing the suppressed-by-contrast behavior we observed in our imaging experiments, and active for all stimulus direction at low contrast but most active for the zero degrees direction, again reproducing VIP neuron tuning (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The external input strength for which VIP neurons are most active corresponds to the highest gain ('supralinear') regime for L2/3 pyramidal and PV activity.
source: The external input strength for which VIP neurons are most active (~10 a.u.) corresponds to the highest gain ('supralinear') regime for L2/3 pyramidal and PV activity (Figure 5d: left).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Ablating the VIP-to-SST inhibitory connection results in a large reduction in the gain and activity of VIP, L2/3 pyramidal, and PV populations at low input.
source: Ablating the VIP-to-SST inhibitory connection, the only output of VIP neurons contained in the model, results in a large reduction in the gain and activity of VIP, L2/3 pyramidal, and PV populations at low input (Figure 5d: right).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Even in the absence of inhibition from VIP neurons, SST neurons have relatively low activity at a low level of external input.
source: Even in the absence of inhibition from VIP neurons, SST neurons have relatively low activity at a low level of external input, demonstrating that suppression of a relatively small amount of SST neuron activity can drive large increases in pyramidal neuron gain.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Suppression of a relatively small amount of SST neuron activity can drive large increases in pyramidal neuron gain.
source: Even in the absence of inhibition from VIP neurons, SST neurons have relatively low activity at a low level of external input, demonstrating that suppression of a relatively small amount of SST neuron activity can drive large increases in pyramidal neuron gain.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: VIP-mediated disinhibition is capable of producing substantial increases in gain at weak inputs, despite low activity of the intermediate SST neuron population, in networks with supralinear single neuron transfer functions and recurrent excitation.
source: These results indicate that VIP-mediated disinhibition is capable of producing substantial increases in gain at weak inputs, despite low activity of the intermediate SST neuron population, in networks with supralinear single neuron transfer functions and recurrent excitation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The network transitions from non-ISN to ISN as external input strength increases with a transition between stability regimes around an external input strength of 50 a.u.
source: We find that the network transitions from non-ISN to ISN as external input strength increases with a transition between stability regimes around an external input strength of 50 a.u. (Figure 5g), as long as the VIP-to-SST connection strength is below a critical value (normalized to be 1.0 in Figure 5g–i).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Above the critical VIP-to-SST connection strength, the network becomes highly unstable even for low external input strengths and firing rates of pyramidal, PV, and VIP neurons explode while SST neuron activity is suppressed.
source: Above the critical VIP-to-SST connection strength, the network becomes highly unstable even for low external input strengths and firing rates of pyramidal, PV, and VIP neurons explode while SST neuron activity is suppressed (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: The gain enhancement is present only at low external input strengths for which the network is in a non-ISN regime, ensuring that the impact of VIP neurons on gain does not disrupt inhibitory stabilization.
source: The gain enhancement is present only at low external input strengths for which the network is in a non-ISN regime, ensuring that the impact of VIP neurons on gain does not disrupt inhibitory stabilization.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5i.

claim: A substantial increase in gain can be achieved over a wide range of VIP-to-SST strengths.
source: Although VIP-mediated disinhibition and increase in network gain can be destabilizing above a critical strength, this analysis demonstrates that a substantial increase in gain can be achieved over a wide range of VIP-to-SST strengths.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The stability behavior and gain effects observed in SSNs with three interneuron populations are robust over a wide range of values for key model parameters.
source: These results demonstrate that the stability behavior and gain effects we observe in SSNs with three interneuron populations are robust over a wide range of values for key model parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5j-l.

claim: At high contrast, SST neuron activity is high, VIP neuron activity is suppressed, and layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron activity is lower than it is at low contrast.
source: This survey of contrast tuning in mouse V1 revealed two distinct regimes of cortical dynamics in superficial layers of cortex. At high contrast, SST neuron activity is high, VIP neuron activity is suppressed, and layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron activity is lower than it is at low contrast; at low contrast, SST neuron activity is low, VIP neuron activity is direction tuned and gated by locomotion, and layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron activity is higher and more enhanced by locomotion.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figures 2-3.

claim: At low contrast, SST neuron activity is low, VIP neuron activity is direction tuned and gated by locomotion, and layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron activity is higher and more enhanced by locomotion.
source: This survey of contrast tuning in mouse V1 revealed two distinct regimes of cortical dynamics in superficial layers of cortex. evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figures 2-3.

claim: SST neurons prefer large gratings, suggestive of a role mediating surround suppression.
source: Measurements of size tuning with high contrast gratings have shown that SST neurons prefer large gratings, suggestive of a role mediating surround suppression, whereas VIP neurons only respond to gratings smaller than those that drive SST neurons (Adesnik et al., 2012; Dipoppa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to Adesnik et al., 2012; Dipoppa et al., 2018.

claim: VIP neurons only respond to gratings smaller than those that drive SST neurons.
source: Measurements of size tuning with high contrast gratings have shown that SST neurons prefer large gratings, suggestive of a role mediating surround suppression, whereas VIP neurons only respond to gratings smaller than those that drive SST neurons (Adesnik et al., 2012; Dipoppa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to Adesnik et al., 2012; Dipoppa et al., 2018.

claim: The receptive fields of VIP neurons are larger than those of SST or pyramidal neurons when measured with sparse noise stimuli.
source: Interestingly, the receptive fields of VIP neurons are larger than those of SST or pyramidal neurons when measured with sparse noise stimuli (de Vries et al., 2020), indicating that the selectivity of VIP neurons for small stimuli does not arise simply from having small linear receptive fields.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to de Vries et al., 2020.

claim: VIP and SST neurons in V1 are tuned for weak and strong inputs, respectively, across multiple stimulus dimensions.
source: This complementary size tuning parallels the complementary contrast tuning observed here, suggesting that VIP and SST neurons in V1 are tuned for weak and strong inputs, respectively, across multiple stimulus dimensions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is an inference based on the contrast and size tuning data.

claim: VIP neurons in mouse primary auditory cortex are selective for lower sound intensities than SST or PV neurons.
source: Indeed, this relationship appears to hold across sensory modalities as VIP neurons in mouse primary auditory cortex are selective for lower sound intensities than SST or PV neurons (Mesik et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to Mesik et al., 2015.

claim: VIP neuron activity supports a high gain regime that increases sensitivity to weak inputs.
source: Taken together, a parsimonious explanation of these results is that VIP neuron activity supports a high gain regime that increases sensitivity to weak inputs, whereas SST neuron activity promotes a low gain regime that decreases sensitivity to strong inputs and maintains network stability.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is an inference based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: SST neuron activity promotes a low gain regime that decreases sensitivity to strong inputs and maintains network stability.

claim: Data was collected using the same data collection pipeline as the Allen Brain Observatory.
source: Data was collected using the same data collection pipeline as the Allen Brain Observatory and processed using the same image processing and event detection methods (See de Vries et al., 2020 for further imaging and image processing details).

claim: Events in the fluorescence trace for each neuron were detected using a changepoint detection algorithm with an L0-regularization penalty.
source: Events in the fluorescence trace for each neuron were detected using a changepoint detection algorithm with an L0-regularization penalty (de Vries et al., 2020; Jewell and Witten, 2018; Jewell et al., 2019).

claim: Individual events likely do not correspond to single action potentials but have a bias toward bursts.
source: The result is a time series of event onset times and magnitudes proportional to the change in GCaMP fluorescence; individual events likely do not correspond to single action potentials but have a bias toward bursts (Ledochowitsch et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: Most, if not all, SST neurons in layer 4 of V1 are Martinotti cells.
source: Notably, most, if not all, SST neurons in layer 4 of V1 are Martinotti cells (Scala et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to Scala et al., 2019.

claim: The stimulus consisted of a full field drifting sinusoidal grating that was presented at a single spatial frequency (0.04 cycles/degree) and temporal frequency (1 Hz), eight directions uniformly distributed in 45 degree increments, and six contrasts (5%, 10%, 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%).
